title: Pascha
hook: Christ is risen! Truly he is risen!

segments.voice: Yesterday, Great Lent, which begins on a Monday after everyone bows and asks forgiveness. Your line was clean monday. Was one meal plainer? Day one thousand three hundred seventy.

Near midnight, and the church is dark. Not dim. Dark. Everyone is holding an unlit candle. Then the priest comes out from behind the icon screen holding a single flame, and the light starts to travel: his candle to the first person's, theirs to the next, until the whole room is gold and flickering. The people follow the priest outside and walk around the church in the night air, singing. They stop at the closed front doors. The priest calls out a short greeting, and the crowd shouts back an answer, loud enough to wake the street. Then the doors open, and Lent is over. Today, the feast those words announce.
screen: `A DARK CHURCH, ONE FLAME.` → `AROUND THE CHURCH, SINGING.` → `THE DOORS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Pascha is what Eastern Christians call Easter. Paul ties it straight to the Passover lamb: in the Douay-Rheims, "For Christ our pasch is sacrificed." The pasch is the Passover. Easter, for these churches, is the new Passover, the night God leads his people from death into life. Next, the greeting. Christ is risen! Truly he is risen! It's said in Greek, Arabic, Ukrainian, Malayalam, Ge'ez, the languages of the churches we've visited. The answer isn't decoration. It echoes the first Easter evening in Luke, when the disciples tell each other, "The Lord is risen indeed." Indeed. Truly. It's a witness, said back. And people keep saying it, as a hello and a goodbye, through the Easter season. Then the hymn they sing outside the doors, which the Byzantine churches repeat over and over: Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death, and giving life to those in the tombs. Last, a sermon, read aloud at the midnight liturgy, attributed to Saint John Chrysostom. It invites everyone to the feast: those who fasted the whole of Lent, and those who came at the last hour, and those who didn't fast at all. Nobody should go away hungry, it says. Nobody should mourn their failings, because forgiveness has risen from the tomb. After a strict Lent, that's not the moment to check who kept the rules. The table is set for all.
screen: `CHRIST OUR PASCH: THE NEW PASSOVER.` · `TRULY HE IS RISEN: A WITNESS SAID BACK.` · `TRAMPLING DOWN DEATH BY DEATH.` · `THE TABLE IS SET FOR ALL.` · then, large: `THE LORD IS RISEN INDEED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse the greeting. Settle, and breathe. Say it quietly to yourself, a few times: Christ is risen. Truly he is risen. Let the second line come a little stronger than the first, the way a crowd answers. Now think of someone you could greet this way at Easter: a friend, a grandparent, someone in a parish hall. Picture their face as they answer. If you pray, the greeting itself can be your prayer. If you don't, hold it as a sentence shouted at midnight in many languages, and notice how it lands. The bell holds the time.
Pascha. The Eastern name for Easter, the new Passover, the feast of Christ's resurrection, opened at midnight with candles and a shouted greeting. Today's word.
Your line: truly he is risen. Today, when someone tells you good news, don't just nod. Say it back to them, stronger. Day one thousand three hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Eastern Catholics celebrate Pascha at a night service with candles, a procession around the church and the repeated greeting "Christ is risen! Truly he is risen!", and use the greeting in place of hello throughout the Easter season.

myth: the answer "truly he is risen" echoes Luke's Gospel
on the first Easter evening the disciples say "the Lord is risen indeed."
the Paschal sermon read at midnight scolds those who didn't fast
it invites everyone to the feast, even those who came at the last hour.
Pascha is linked to the Passover
Paul writes "Christ our pasch is sacrificed": the pasch is the Passover lamb.

fork.setup: it's Easter week. an Eastern Catholic friend greets you: "Christ is risen!" what's the traditional reply?
fork.reveal: "truly he is risen!" the answer is a witness said back, echoing the disciples in Luke: the Lord is risen indeed.

original.note: Greek: Christ is risen, the Easter greeting; the reply is Ἀληθῶς ἀνέστη, truly he is risen.

trapdoor: what you thought: Pascha is just a foreign word for Easter.
what it means: the feast of the resurrection as the new Passover, opened at midnight with a greeting answered by the whole church.
what a scholar hears: in the Douay-Rheims, 1 Corinthians 5:7 names Christ the pasch, the Passover sacrifice, and the Byzantine troparion proclaims death trampled down by death.

sources.quoted: For Christ our pasch is sacrificed.

sources.ref: Paschal homily attributed to Saint John Chrysostom

notes: Paschal troparion given in a common English form ('Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death, and giving life to those in the tombs') without quotation marks, since English wordings vary. Confirm it is acceptable as a description.
Paschal homily of Chrysostom summarized, not quoted. Confirm the summary.
The greeting's use 'for the whole Easter season' (until Ascension in Byzantine practice): confirm.
Midnight service description (dark church, light from behind the iconostasis, procession, closed doors) follows common Byzantine practice; details vary. Confirm.
The link between Pascha and Passover is made through 1 Corinthians 5:7 rather than an etymology. Confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording of 1 Corinthians 5:7 and Luke 24:34: confirm.
Original: Χριστὸς ἀνέστη / Ἀληθῶς ἀνέστη; confirm accents and pronunciation.

Editor: fixed a wrong count in the hook ('three words' answered by 'three of their own': the English reply 'Truly he is risen' has four, the Greek two); cut the unsourced 'it is an old name'; 'the very first' and 'the whole Easter season' softened; teach opener varied.
